content:
Dear all,
In the CSLib SG, we've been discussing a change to the copyright header to make decisions more straightforward for contributors when they add new files or edit an existing file significantly.

The new proposed policy is to have the header look like this (still working on the precise formulation of the first line)

Copyright (c) 2026 the authors (see below). All rights reserved.
Released under Apache 2.0 license as described in the file LICENSE.
Authors: Alice, Bob, Carol

The significant change is the first line, which will always be the same for all files.
The Authors field is as before, but we'll adopt the practice of making it alphabetically ordered. Its purpose, which we will state explicitly in the repo's guidelines, is simply to track who owns copyrights of parts of the file.

I'd like to get some feedback on this, so please give it a thumbs up or thumbs down, and please feel free to comment below.

In mathlib, the two lines play different roles - the first is the copyright holder, and the second is the authors, ie people to be contacted in case of confusion or maintenance problems. It's true that these can coincide, but for some - particularly older - files, it's useful for these people to be distinct. So I'd suggest thinking about what the purpose of these lines is - this isn't to disagree with the proposal though!

On a technical note, I'd ask that the wording please remain compatible with the header linter. It's fairly lenient about the first line, so the above works for instance.

Bhavik said already what I was typing out: the author's line is about who to contact for maintenance. In particular, I'd prefer that not every commit to a file necessitates adding yourself to this. For instance, I often make small changes to files that are purely technical, where listing me would be unhelpful.

I think in practice that it's probably fine to consolidate this into one line with an early project, I'd just reserve the right to later move someone from the author's line to the top if we need this distinction later.

The mathlib standard of authorship is highly inadequate for computer science. We are a more artifact heavy field where authorship and copyright of artifacts needs to belong to the correct person. The word "author" carries a specific meaning across ~two dozen subfields with their own publication bodies (such as SIG groups or their non-American equivalents like EATCS), that a single open source repository cannot change. In the current CSLib setup, an author of a near-duplicate PR can claim copyright for themselves or their employer. This can create insurmountable headaches at CS venues. Note that every subfield of CS has its own strange collection of norms and rituals for publication. Most mathlib related papers land at a very small subset of them which are all relatively small single-blind conferences. Thus verifying authorship trails of upstream artefacts is trivial at these venues.

On a different note : It is a terrible idea to associate authorship with maintenance since the original authors might disappear. Then either they are listed as author but not available for maintenance or, their name is removed from the author list, which creates a false record. As it is, I think Fabrizio's proposal explicitly suggests only including author names where they have made substantial contributions.

The correct way to track the maintainer for a file should be something akin to an
"active maintainer list" in the copyright header.

Another option would be to take the approach used by formal-conjectures, and use "the CSLib authors" as the copyright line, (optionally maintaining a separateAUTHORS file at the root of the repository). Tracking copyright per file is pretty silly in mathlib where files are split, merged, and extended all the time.

I think that would result in legal conundrums. Recently, a well-known paper had a problem with ACM due to copyright laws requiring de-anonymised names and addresses. Even the PC chair could not persuade ACM to forgo this step. The authors could not just sign off as "authors of <insert project name>" or "<list of authors>, and anonymous authors of the <project>". If artefacts become part of the publication, as is already becoming the norm, then the copyrights of the artefact might also have to be tied to the correct individuals.

@Eric Wieser - this proposal does sound appealing and it is also the approach we use for the tools developed in my lab, but I don't think it will work well for CSLlib, where I expect we will have many contributors, each touching only a few files. Imagine we lump hundreds of contributors together in one big AUTHORS file and give them all the copyright for all of CSLib. I don't think people would be happy with that solution. Tracking on a per-file basis seems best. It does require some effort when files are modified or split or rearranged, but I would argue that this is effort that should be done so that we don't lose track of who contributed. I do feel strongly that giving credit for work in CSLib is essential to its success.

One other note - commenting on a point raised above - we agreed in the SC that putting your name on a file's author list is something that should be done only if a "significant contribution" is made. Generally, we would like contributors to make that judgement call and add themselves to the author list if they feel they have made a significant contribution. Hopefully, people will be reasonable and not add themselves if they fix a typo or make some other minor fix.

Many files in the Lean repository have a copyright header which looks like

/-
Copyright (c) 2026 Lean FRO, LLC. All rights reserved.
Released under Apache 2.0 license as described in the file LICENSE.
Author: Julia Markus Himmel
-/

because while we are "on the clock", the code that Lean FRO employees write has its copyright assigned to the Lean FRO. I think this is the norm for software engineers.

This raises the question what someone who is under such a contract would put in the proposed CSLib copyright header.

I’m generally very confused about the copyright field. How can a single person hold the copyright to a file that is edited by many people? Also, as long as there is no other identifying information apart from the name, how can this be legally relevant? I’m much in favour of either assigning copyright to a governing body (which also makes things like license decisions, legal battles etc much easier) or using the solution proposed in the first post to this thread. Also the file does live in a git repository that has further author information attached (although I don’t know if that disappears on a merge)
I guess in theory every author should add a new additional copyright line for new contributions, but certainly Mathlib has not been doing that

Eric Wieser said:

I guess in theory every author should add a new additional copyright line for new contributions, but certainly Mathlib has not been doing that

Per Apache license this is required. See point 4c and related point 4d. I guess it’s one of those loosely enforced provisions.

Thanks for all the comments so far. A few notes:

  • The purpose of the 'Authors' field would be to register who has made significant contributions to the file, not maintenance. We're trying to fix an attribution problem here, which seems problematic if there's a single person at the top. We can consider adding a way to track contact people, but I'd keep it separate (and maybe tracking this per file is not the best?... To be discussed.)
  • Everyone who makes a contribution to a file has copyright to their code (as long as it's original; I doubt changing whitespaces counts).
  • When splitting files, we'll have the problem of reporting the right authors. I think this is still better than just ignoring the problem.
  • I guess it'd be ok to list an entity in the Authors field (e.g., Lean FRO). I'd be ok with name and affiliation as well, e.g., 'Carol Doe (Lean FRO)'.
  • Clark summarised very well why we didn't think having a global AUTHOR file and a single 'CSLib Contributors' header would work.
  • Re using a single entity in all files, like 'the CSLib FRO' (if such a thing existed). I don't like this because it'd require asking people to sign off their copyright to such entity. An upside is that the license can be easily changed by the entity if 'necessary'. But this is also a huge downside (depending on the point of view)! The other advantages mentioned (legal battles, etc.) are true, but I think some of them can be taken up by an org anyway.
I second the solution of copyright "(author name) (affiliation org)” to the organisation copyright issue, since this is how we record authorship on papers in academia.

I seems to me that we should first be educated on what being a copyright holder of a file in an open-source project under the Apache 2.0 license actually means legally in terms of rights and obligations and possible future economic consequences.

In https://llvm.org/docs/DeveloperPolicy.html, they note that copyright is held by the contributors, which I believe implicitly means that those who have contributed to a file implicitly hold copyright. They do not have a copyright notice in files. To me, this seems much easier than litigating contentious copyright issues in-tree.

I realise now that my formulation about copyright was a bit misleading in my last message. Anyone who made an original contribution (even if very small) to a file has copyright over the code they wrote, of course. I've revised it.

Perhaps it's good to mention some things that I think are worth balancing:

  • A relatively straightforward process that doesn't overload us with discussing attribution.
  • Giving people proper attribution.
  • Making people not rush to creating files or PRs, but instead encourage calm discussion and collaboration.
  • Making it easy to track who has copyright in CSLib. (Git history is not a complete solution to this.)

All while being correct in our use of the license (this is a must). Suggestions (like some already given) are welcome, especially because some of these aspects are a bit vague in nature.

An example about git history being incomplete, if necessary: sometimes people do pair programming and it's up to the person at the keyboard to report correctly the right Authors in the file.
@Fabrizio Montesi Have you compared this to the copyright policies with other big projects? mathlib? lean itself? AFP? math-comp? rocq stdlib...?

Fabrizio Montesi said:

An example about git history being incomplete, if necessary: sometimes people do pair programming and it's up to the person at the keyboard to report correctly the right Authors in the file.

If we can rely on contributors to add their collaborators to Authors, then why can we not rely on them to write Co-authored-by in the commit message?

The last time I tried it, it took me several times to get it right until GitHub recognised authorship. That suggests that git co-authoring is a painfully brittle system.

Secondly authorship is also about visibility. If the word “authors” appears in the top of a file, it must list all authors. This is for the same reason we insist on not using et al. citations in some venues.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Co-authoring is a painfully brittle system

Wouldn't this be easy to lint against and warn, like mathilb does for PR titles?

I think if we're going to say that every substantial change requires a change to the copyright header, we should be very clear what counts as "maintenance" or not. My suspicion is the current proposal means we'll get copyright lines cluttered up by trivial changes, when the people making real refactors across the library sensibly decide not to update 100s of copyright lines at once, despite their contributions being more valuable.

It's simply doing too much to try to have a single data field record "who is responsible for this file" and "who has ever touched it".

That’s not a part of the proposal though. The proposal adds a general line saying that copyright belongs to the author list. Nothing changes there when a file changes. The only changes are in the author list. The retention of prior copyright notices in derivative work is a requirement of the Apache 2.0 license, not the proposal. Copyright claims going to people who “make original contributions however small” is just the standard practice. It’s not exactly legally optional.

Further maintenance issues can be alleviated by adding an explicit list of maintainers to the header, and managing it is trivial with a set of scripts.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

The last time I tried it, it took me several times to get it right until GitHub recognised authorship.

I don't think it matters all that much whether GitHub recognizes it. Certainly GitHub does not recognize the "authors" comments.
Yes but the authors comments are visible to anyone who opens the file, which is also important.

Another possible change suggestion : adopt the llvm policy and simply relabel the “authors” field to “maintainers” in Fabrizio’s proposed header, and a commitment to add all authors in the git history.
